title: How to Earn Money on Fiverr as a Beginner
excerpt: Fiverr is one of the easiest places to earn your first money online — if you set up your profile and gigs the right way. Here is the full beginner process, from choosing a service to getting your first order.
coverAlt: A freelancer working at a desk with a laptop, notebook and coffee
haystack:
how to earn money on fiverr as a beginner fiverr is one of the easiest places to earn your first money online — if you set up your profile and gigs the right way. here is the full beginner process, from choosing a service to getting your first order. fiverr freelancing earning platforms earning platforms ## what fiverr is and how it works

fiverr is a marketplace where freelancers sell services — called gigs — and buyers come to find them. instead of applying for jobs, you list what you can do, set a price, and buyers order from you. services range from writing and graphic design to voiceovers, video editing, data entry, and virtual assistance.

when a buyer orders, fiverr holds the payment. you deliver the work, the buyer accepts it (or asks for a revision), and fiverr releases the money to you after a clearance period. fiverr takes a 20% commission on each order, so a $50 order earns you $40. factor that into your pricing from the start.

## what beginners can sell on fiverr

you do not need ten years of experience. beginners do well with services that are quick to learn and easy to deliver:

- writing: product descriptions, social media captions, blog outlines, proofreading.
- design: social media posts, simple logos, presentation slides, using tools like canva.
- admin help: data entry, spreadsheets, research, virtual assistance.
- audio and video: voiceovers, podcast editing, short video captions.
- simple tech tasks: wordpress fixes, spreadsheet formulas, file conversions.

pick one service you can already do reasonably well, or one you can learn in a week of focused practice. trying to sell ten unrelated services at once is the most common beginner mistake.

## setting up a profile buyers trust

buyers choose sellers they trust. a strong profile has:

- a real photo of you, or a clean professional logo — not a stock image.
- a one-line description that says what you do and who it is for, for example "i write clear product descriptions for online shops".
- a short bio that mentions your skills, the tools you use, and how fast you reply.
- your language skills and time zone, so buyers know when to expect answers.

fill in every section. empty profiles look unfinished, and buyers skip them.

## creating your first gig

a gig is your shop listing. each one needs:

- a clear title that says the service and the result, for example "i will write 5 product descriptions for your online store".
- a description that explains exactly what the buyer gets, how many revisions are included, and what you need from them to start.
- a cover image that shows the work, not just text on a coloured background. if you have no past work yet, create one or two sample pieces to show.
- delivery time you can actually meet. a 2-day delivery you hit is better than a 1-day delivery you miss.

fiverr lets you create several gigs, but start with one or two and make them good.

## pricing your first gigs

new sellers usually start low to win their first orders and reviews. that does not mean working for almost nothing — it means pricing below the established sellers in your category while you build a track record.

a practical approach: set your basic package at a price that feels slightly low but still worth your time, and offer standard and premium packages with more work for more money. as reviews arrive, raise your prices gradually. sellers who never raise prices stay stuck at beginner rates.

## getting your first order

fiverr's search favours gigs that are complete, active, and responsive. to get your first order:

- stay online and reply to messages quickly — response time matters for search ranking.
- share your gig where buyers already gather: relevant social media groups, forums, and your own profiles.
- consider the "buyer requests" section, where buyers post jobs they need done and sellers can offer their services.
- ask a past client or a friend who genuinely used your service to leave an honest review after a real order — never buy fake reviews, which can get your account banned.

your first few orders are the hardest. after five to ten completed orders with good reviews, new orders start coming in more easily.

## fiverr fees and realistic expectations

be honest with yourself about the numbers. fiverr takes 20% of every order. withdrawal options and their fees vary by country and method, so check what applies to you before you need the money. payments take time to clear after delivery.

fiverr will not make you rich in a week. most beginners earn small amounts at first — a few orders a month — and grow from there. what it does give you is a place to earn your first money online, build a portfolio of real client work, and learn what buyers actually pay for.

## growing beyond your first orders

fiverr has seller levels. new sellers can progress to level one, level two, and top rated by completing orders on time, keeping high ratings, and staying responsive. higher levels unlock more gigs, better placement in search, and extra tools.

to grow: deliver on time, communicate clearly, ask satisfied buyers for a review, and keep improving the service itself. one happy buyer who returns every month is worth far more than ten one-off orders.

## mistakes beginners make

- copying another seller's gig text word for word. buyers notice, and fiverr can remove copied listings.
- accepting work you cannot do, then delivering late or badly. one bad review early on is hard to recover from.
- ignoring messages for days. slow replies push your gig down in search.
- underpricing permanently. low prices win first orders, but raise them as your reviews grow.
- treating fiverr as the whole business. use it to find clients and build a reputation — and keep your own portfolio and client list outside the platform too.

## is fiverr worth it for a beginner?

if you have a service people will pay for and you are willing to start small, yes. it is one of the few places where a complete beginner can get a first paying client without a portfolio, a website, or a professional network. the trade-off is the 20% commission and the competition. go in with realistic expectations, deliver good work, and treat your first ten orders as the foundation — not the finish line.

title: Common Online Earning Scams and How to Avoid Them
excerpt: If earning money online were as easy as the adverts claim, everyone would be rich. Learn the patterns scammers reuse, so you can spot them in seconds.
coverAlt: Illustration of a warning sign in front of suspicious messages
haystack:
common online earning scams and how to avoid them if earning money online were as easy as the adverts claim, everyone would be rich. learn the patterns scammers reuse, so you can spot them in seconds. scams safety beginners side hustles ## the golden rule

a legitimate way to earn money online never asks you to pay money to start earning, never guarantees income, and never pressures you to decide in minutes. if an opportunity breaks any of those rules, walk away.

## scam patterns to recognise

### pay to start

"you just need to pay a $50 registration fee / buy the starter pack / pay for training." real employers pay you; you do not pay them. training costs exist in some legitimate fields, but they are never a condition of a job offer that arrived out of nowhere.

### guaranteed income

"make $500 a day from your phone, guaranteed." no honest business can guarantee your income. guarantees are a marketing claim, not a fact — and in most cases they are simply false.

### the overpayment / cheque scam

a "client" sends you a cheque for too much money and asks you to send the difference back. the cheque later bounces, and you have lost the money you sent. never accept overpayment, and never send money to a client.

### fake tasks and crypto doubling

tasks that pay you to like posts, or schemes that promise to double your cryptocurrency, are almost always fraud or money laundering. your account, and in some cases your legal liability, is the price.

### stolen job listings

scammers copy real job adverts, change the contact details, and "hire" you — then ask for identity documents or bank details. always apply through the employer's official careers page, and verify the recruiter's identity independently.

## how to verify any opportunity

1. search the company or scheme name with the word "scam" or "review".
2. check the website's age, contact details, and whether the company is registered where it claims to be.
3. never send identity documents or bank details to someone who contacted you first.
4. ask a trusted person, or a professional community, before paying anything.

## if you have been scammed

stop sending money immediately, keep every message and receipt, report it to your bank and to your country's fraud reporting service, and change any passwords you shared. reporting helps others — scammers rely on silence.

## the boring truth

legitimate earning online is slow, skill-based, and uncertain at first. that is not a flaw in the honest opportunities; it is the reason the scams look so attractive. the safest earning route is the one you can explain to a sceptical friend in one sentence — and that friend would believe.

title: How to Choose a Profitable Digital Skill
excerpt: Not every in-demand skill is a good fit for you. Choose by combining market demand, how fast you can learn it, and whether you will enjoy doing it for clients.
coverAlt: Illustration of different skill paths branching from a single starting point
haystack:
how to choose a profitable digital skill not every in-demand skill is a good fit for you. choose by combining market demand, how fast you can learn it, and whether you will enjoy doing it for clients. digital skills career learning digital skills ## the three questions

a skill is worth learning for earning if it passes three tests:

1. **do clients pay for it?** look at job listings and freelance marketplaces. if almost nobody is hiring for it, it is a hobby, not an income skill — for now.
2. **can you learn it in months, not years?** some skills, like data analysis or video editing, have a usable beginner level. others, like advanced software engineering, take longer to reach a billable standard.
3. **will you enjoy the work?** you will spend hundreds of hours practising. a skill you dislike is one you will abandon.

## skills with steady demand

demand changes, so check current listings rather than trusting a list. as a starting point, these categories consistently appear in hiring and freelance demand:

| category | examples | time to first paid work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| writing and content | copywriting, seo writing, technical writing | weeks to months |
| design | graphic design, ui design, video editing | months |
| data | spreadsheets, data analysis, dashboards | months |
| marketing | social media management, email marketing, paid ads | months |
| development | web development, no-code tools, automation | months to a year |

## how to check demand yourself

do not trust a course that says a skill is "in demand". check it:

- search freelance marketplaces for the skill and count active jobs.
- read job listings and note the tools they require.
- look at the rates posted, and whether jobs are one-off or recurring.

## learning without wasting money

start with free, high-quality material: official documentation, free courses from reputable providers, and practice projects. pay for a course only when you know what it teaches that the free material does not, and when you have already started practising.

## getting to your first paid job

learn in public: publish your practice work, help in communities, and offer a small paid project to a real client as soon as your work is good enough — not perfect. the first paid job teaches you more about the market than another month of tutorials.

## reassess every year

skills age. a tool that is essential today may be automated tomorrow. keep one eye on how your skill is changing, and keep learning the parts that machines do badly: judgement, taste, communication, and understanding what a client actually needs.

title: How to Start a Faceless YouTube Channel
excerpt: You do not have to appear on camera to build a YouTube channel. Faceless channels use narration, screen recordings, and animation — but they still need original value.
coverAlt: A video editing timeline on a screen with a play button
haystack:
how to start a faceless youtube channel you do not have to appear on camera to build a youtube channel. faceless channels use narration, screen recordings, and animation — but they still need original value. youtube video monetisation youtube earning ## what "faceless" actually means

a faceless channel is one where the creator does not appear on camera. the video might use a voiceover, screen recording, animation, stock footage, or text on screen. the creator is still doing the work — researching, scripting, editing — and the channel still needs original value to grow.

## choose a format you can sustain

formats that work without a presenter include:

- **explainers:** a scripted voiceover with visuals that illustrate each point.
- **tutorials:** screen recordings showing how to do something, step by step.
- **documentary-style:** narration over footage and graphics.
- **lists and comparisons:** structured, well-researched rankings.

pick one format and one topic. a channel about everything grows slower than a channel about one thing done well.

## the equipment you actually need

a decent microphone matters more than a camera you will not use. a quiet room, a script, and free or low-cost editing software are enough to start. spend money on audio before anything else — viewers forgive plain visuals, but they leave videos they cannot hear clearly.

## monetisation requirements

youtube's partner programme has eligibility requirements that change over time — currently based on subscribers and watch hours, or on shorts views. check the current requirements in youtube's official help centre before planning around them. beyond ads, faceless channels can earn from affiliate links, sponsorships, and their own products, but those also depend on audience trust.

## what youtube does not reward

reused, low-effort content — slideshows of stock images with a robotic voice reading scraped text — is routinely demonetised or removed. youtube's policies on reused content and spam are strict, and channels built on copied material rarely last. original scripting and editing are the work; the "faceless" part is only about the camera.

## a realistic first 20 videos

1. pick your topic and format.
2. write scripts before recording anything.
3. publish on a schedule you can keep — weekly is realistic.
4. study your retention graphs: where do viewers leave, and why?
5. improve one thing per video — the hook, the pacing, the audio, the thumbnail.

most channels grow slowly for months. the creators who succeed are the ones who keep publishing while the numbers are small.

title: How to Sell Digital Products
excerpt: Templates, presets, guides, and courses can earn income long after you make them — but only if they solve a specific problem for a specific buyer.
coverAlt: A workspace with a laptop showing a digital product storefront
haystack:
how to sell digital products templates, presets, guides, and courses can earn income long after you make them — but only if they solve a specific problem for a specific buyer. digital products online business passive income digital products ## what counts as a digital product

anything a customer can download or access online: a spreadsheet template, a design template, a preset pack, an ebook, a short course, a set of icons, a notion system. the product is made once and sold many times, which is why the margins are attractive — and why the competition is real.

## start with a problem, not a product

the products that sell answer a question a buyer is already asking: "how do i invoice clients?", "how do i plan a wedding on a budget?", "how do i edit photos faster?" ask in communities, read reviews of competing products, and note what buyers complain is missing.

## validate before you build

before spending weeks on a product, test the idea:

1. describe it in one paragraph and share it where your audience is.
2. offer a simple version or a pre-order to ten people.
3. if nobody is interested, change the idea — not the marketing.

## where to sell

marketplaces bring built-in traffic and take a fee; your own website keeps more of the price but needs you to bring the buyers. many sellers start on a marketplace to learn what sells, then move their best products to their own store.

## pricing

price by the value to the buyer, not by your hours. a template that saves a freelancer an hour a week is worth more than a template that saves ten minutes once. look at comparable products, then price in the same range until you have reviews — and raise the price when the product improves.

## what buyers expect

- a clear description of exactly what is included, with screenshots or a preview.
- files that work as described, with instructions.
- a way to contact you if something does not work.
- a refund policy stated upfront. digital products have higher refund expectations than many sellers assume, so be clear about what you offer.

## the honest truth about "passive" income

digital products are not passive at the start. you will spend far more time making, listing, and promoting the product than you will spend on each sale. the income becomes steadier only after you have an audience, good reviews, and a product that people recommend.

title: How to Find Legitimate Remote Jobs
excerpt: Real remote jobs exist — and so do thousands of fake listings. Learn where to look, how employers actually hire, and the red flags that mean walk away.
coverAlt: Illustration of a person working from home at a laptop with a video call on screen
haystack:
how to find legitimate remote jobs real remote jobs exist — and so do thousands of fake listings. learn where to look, how employers actually hire, and the red flags that mean walk away. remote jobs work from home job search online jobs ## where legitimate remote jobs are listed

start with the places employers actually use: company careers pages, established job boards with remote filters, and specialist remote job boards. recruitment agencies that specialise in remote work are also worth contacting. be wary of listings that only appear on social media posts or messaging apps.

## how real hiring works

a legitimate employer will:

- interview you, usually by video, before offering a job.
- give you a written contract or offer letter.
- pay you through a normal payroll or payment system.
- never ask you to pay for training, equipment, or a "processing fee" to start.

if any of those are missing, pause and investigate.

## red flags that mean a listing is probably a scam

- you are offered a job without an interview.
- the salary is far above the market rate for the role.
- you are asked to pay money upfront, buy equipment from a specific seller, or cash cheques.
- the employer's email is a free webmail address and there is no verifiable company website.
- the job description is vague, full of spelling errors, or copied from elsewhere.
- you are contacted on whatsapp or telegram by someone claiming to be a recruiter, with no linkedin profile or company email.

see our full guide to online earning scams for more detail on each of these.

## preparing a remote-ready application

remote employers look for evidence you can work without supervision:

- a cv that states your tools and time zone clearly.
- examples of work, even from personal projects.
- a short cover note that answers the job's actual requirements, not a generic template.
- reliable internet and a quiet place to work — mention it if the job asks.

## the application routine

apply to a focused list of roles you genuinely fit, rather than spraying hundreds of generic applications. tailor the first paragraph of each application to the role, follow up once after a week, and keep a simple spreadsheet of where you applied and when.

## what to do if you are unsure

search the company name plus "scam" or "review", check the domain's age and registration, and ask in a professional community. if something feels wrong, it usually is — a real employer will not mind you verifying them.

title: How to Start a Blog
excerpt: Starting a blog is easy. Starting a blog people read takes a topic, a publishing habit, and patience. This guide covers the practical setup and the first ten posts.
coverAlt: Illustration of a blog article being written, with headings and an image
haystack:
how to start a blog starting a blog is easy. starting a blog people read takes a topic, a publishing habit, and patience. this guide covers the practical setup and the first ten posts. blogging seo beginners blogging ## pick a topic narrow enough to win

"the best laptops" is a topic you will not rank for as a beginner. "laptops for architecture students on a budget" is a topic you might. a narrow topic lets you write the best answer on the internet for a specific reader — and that is how small blogs grow.

## choose a platform

you need a platform you control, with your own domain name. free hosted platforms are fine for practice, but if you want the blog to earn money later, own the domain and be able to move your content. keep the setup simple: a fast theme, a clear structure, and analytics you actually look at.

## the technical setup, briefly

- **domain:** short, memorable, and easy to spell out loud.
- **hosting:** any reliable shared or cloud host with backups.
- **speed:** a lightweight theme, compressed images, and no unnecessary plugins.
- **structure:** categories for your main topics, and a clear url pattern such as /category/article-slug/.

## plan your first ten posts

before publishing, write down ten article ideas that answer real questions people search for. each post should target one question and answer it better than the current results. a good first list mixes:

- beginner guides ("how to…")
- comparisons ("x vs y")
- lists with real criteria ("best x for…")
- answers to specific questions

## writing for readers and search

write the answer first, then the background. use headings that match the questions readers ask, short paragraphs, and examples. add internal links to your own related posts — it helps readers and search engines understand your site.

do not write for search engines at the expense of readers. the sites that last are the ones people return to.

## how blogs earn money

common routes, in order of realism for a new blog:

1. **affiliate links** in genuinely useful articles.
2. **display ads**, once traffic is meaningful.
3. **your own products or services**, once you have an audience that trusts you.
4. **sponsorships**, once brands can see your reach.

none of these work without traffic, and traffic follows useful content published consistently.

## a realistic schedule

one good post a week beats five rushed posts. publish weekly for six months before judging the blog. most blogs that fail do so because they stop in month two.

title: Affiliate Marketing Explained for Beginners
excerpt: Affiliate marketing means recommending products you have researched and earning a commission when someone buys through your link. Here is how it works — and what it does not do.
coverAlt: Illustration of a recommendation linking a reader to a product
haystack:
affiliate marketing explained for beginners affiliate marketing means recommending products you have researched and earning a commission when someone buys through your link. here is how it works — and what it does not do. affiliate marketing beginners blogging affiliate marketing ## what affiliate marketing is

when you join an affiliate programme, you get a unique link for a product or service. if someone clicks your link and buys, you earn a commission — usually a percentage of the sale. the buyer pays the same price.

it is a real business model, but it is not passive income on day one. you need an audience that trusts you, and content that helps them decide.

## how people actually earn

most affiliate income comes from one of three places:

- **reviews and comparisons:** "best x for y" articles that compare real options.
- **tutorials:** guides that show how to use a product to solve a problem.
- **recommendations inside useful content:** a tool mentioned because it is genuinely the right tool for the job.

what does not work well is a page of links with no useful content. search engines and readers both ignore it.

## getting started

1. **pick a topic you know.** finance tools, software, courses, and physical products all have affiliate programmes — but you need to understand the topic to recommend well.
2. **build the content first.** a blog, youtube channel, or newsletter with genuinely useful material comes before the links.
3. **apply to programmes.** start with the programmes of products you already use. large networks exist, but direct programmes often pay better and give better support.
4. **disclose clearly.** every page with affiliate links must say so, in plain language, near the top. this is a legal requirement in many countries, and it is also how you keep trust.

## choosing what to promote

ask three questions before promoting anything:

- would i recommend this if there were no commission?
- have i used it, or researched it thoroughly?
- is the commission structure clear, and does the company pay reliably?

if the answer to any of these is no, do not promote it.

## mistakes beginners make

- promoting too many products, so nothing is credible.
- writing reviews of products they have never tried.
- hiding the disclosure in small print at the bottom.
- expecting income in the first month. affiliate income usually follows audience growth, which takes months.

## a realistic timeline

months one to three are for content and learning. months three to six may bring the first small commissions. sustainable income, if it comes, usually follows a year or more of consistent, honest publishing. anyone promising faster results is selling a course, not a fact.

title: How to Build an Online Portfolio
excerpt: A portfolio is not a gallery of everything you have done. It is a short argument: here is the problem, here is what I did, here is the result.
coverAlt: Illustration of a portfolio page with project thumbnails arranged in a grid
haystack:
how to build an online portfolio a portfolio is not a gallery of everything you have done. it is a short argument: here is the problem, here is what i did, here is the result. portfolio freelancing career digital skills ## what a portfolio is for

a client or hiring manager spends seconds deciding whether to keep looking. your portfolio has one job in those seconds: show the kind of work they need, done well. everything else is decoration.

## choose three to six projects

fewer, stronger projects beat a long list. for each project, include:

- **the brief:** what the client or problem was, in one or two sentences.
- **your role:** what you actually did, not what the team did.
- **the result:** what changed — more signups, a faster process, a clearer message. if you do not have numbers, describe the outcome honestly instead of inventing them.
- **the work itself:** images, links, or documents a visitor can inspect.

if you have no client work yet, make self-initiated projects: redesign a local business's flyer, write a sample article series, build a small website for a fictional shop. label them clearly as personal projects.

## structure that works

a simple structure is enough:

1. a short introduction — who you are and what you do.
2. your best three projects, with a short case study each.
3. a list of services and tools.
4. testimonials, only if they are real and attributed.
5. a clear way to contact you.

## design and technical basics

- make it load fast and work on a phone; most visitors will be on mobile.
- use real text, not images of text, so search engines and screen readers can read it.
- keep navigation to one page or a handful of pages. a portfolio that is hard to navigate is a portfolio that is not read.
- add your name, location (if you are comfortable), and email on every page.

## keep it current

review your portfolio every three months. remove work that no longer represents you, add your best recent project, and update your services. an out-of-date portfolio quietly tells visitors you have stopped improving.

## common mistakes

- showing everything, including weak early work.
- no context — images with no explanation of the brief or your role.
- broken links and slow-loading images.
- no contact details, or a contact form that nobody answers.

a good portfolio does not need to be fancy. it needs to be honest, focused, and easy to use.

title: Best AI Tools for Freelancers
excerpt: AI tools can speed up drafting, research, and admin — if you stay in charge of quality. Here is how freelancers are actually using them.
coverAlt: A laptop screen showing an AI assistant helping draft a document
haystack:
best ai tools for freelancers ai tools can speed up drafting, research, and admin — if you stay in charge of quality. here is how freelancers are actually using them. ai tools freelancing productivity ai earning ## what ai tools are actually good for

ai tools are strongest at first drafts, summaries, and repetitive work. they are weakest at judgement: knowing what a client actually wants, what is true, and what is good taste. use them for the first 70% of a task, then bring your own expertise to the last 30%.

## tools freelancers use every day

### writing and editing

general-purpose ai assistants can draft outlines, rewrite awkward sentences, and summarise long documents. they also invent facts confidently, so every claim in client work must be checked against a real source. never paste a client's confidential material into a tool without checking its privacy terms.

### research

ai search tools can gather background quickly, but they are a starting point, not a source. follow the links, read the original page, and cite that — not the ai summary.

### design and images

image generators are useful for mockups, mood boards, and placeholder art. for final client work, check the tool's licence terms and the client's policy on ai-generated images before delivering.

### audio and video

transcription tools turn interviews and meetings into searchable text. ai editing tools can cut silences and generate captions, which saves hours on video work.

### admin

ai can draft invoices, proposal templates, and follow-up emails. keep a human review step: a wrong price or a wrong name in an automated email costs more than the time it saved.

## how to charge for ai-assisted work

clients pay for the result, not for the hours you spent. if a tool lets you deliver faster, that is a reason to take on more work or improve quality — not a reason to cut your price in half. be transparent if a client asks how the work was produced, and never present ai output as original research or original photography.

## a simple workflow

1. brief the tool with the client's goal, audience, and constraints.
2. generate a draft, then rewrite it in the client's voice.
3. check every fact, name, number, and link.
4. run your own quality pass before delivery.

## what to avoid

- delivering unedited ai output as finished work.
- using ai to fake expertise you do not have.
- uploading client data to tools with unclear data policies.
- building your whole business on one tool's pricing or availability.

ai tools reward freelancers who already know their craft. learn the skill first; let the tool remove the repetitive parts.

title: How to Start Freelancing as a Beginner
excerpt: Freelancing rewards clarity: one service, one audience, one way to get paid. This guide walks through the first month, step by step.
coverAlt: A freelancer working at a desk with a laptop, notebook, and coffee
haystack:
how to start freelancing as a beginner freelancing rewards clarity: one service, one audience, one way to get paid. this guide walks through the first month, step by step. freelancing beginners clients freelancing ## start with one service, not ten

new freelancers often list every skill they have. clients do the opposite: they search for one specific problem solved well. pick the service you can already deliver to a decent standard — writing, design, video editing, data entry, virtual assistance, translation — and make that your offer.

write it down in one sentence: "i help [who] do [what] so they get [result]." if you cannot fill in the blanks, you are not ready to pitch yet.

## set up the basics before you look for clients

you need four things before your first pitch:

- **a way to be paid.** a bank account or payment service that works in your country, and a simple invoice template.
- **a portfolio, even a small one.** three sample pieces beat an empty profile. create them for fictional clients if you have no real ones yet, and label them as samples.
- **a rate.** research what others charge for similar work in your market, then price by project or by hour — and write the rate down before a client asks.
- **a contract habit.** even a short email confirming scope, deadline, revisions, and payment terms prevents most disputes.

## where to find your first clients

there are three realistic routes, and most beginners should try all three:

| route | how it works | watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| freelance marketplaces | clients post jobs; you bid | high competition, platform fees |
| direct outreach | you email businesses that need your service | low reply rates at first |
| your own network | former colleagues, local businesses, friends | small at first, but converts best |

on marketplaces, your first reviews matter more than your first paycheque. a small, well-delivered job that earns a good review is worth more than a larger job that ends badly.

## how to price your first jobs

start by estimating the hours a job will take, multiply by a modest hourly rate, and add a margin for revisions and communication. if a client wants a fixed price, agree the scope in writing first — "one logo, two revision rounds, delivered in five days" — so the price has a boundary.

raise your rate after every three to five successful jobs, or when you are turning work away. that is the market telling you that you are underpriced.

## common beginner mistakes

- **saying yes to everything.** a bad-fit client costs more time than the fee is worth.
- **working without a deposit.** for new clients, ask for part of the fee upfront.
- **no boundaries.** agree working hours and revision limits in advance.
- **hiding your work.** share what you make. clients hire people they have seen do the work.

## your first month, in order

1. choose one service and write your one-sentence offer.
2. make three portfolio samples.
3. create profiles on one or two marketplaces and a simple personal page.
4. send five tailored pitches a day for two weeks.
